newsitem.title: USA: Simpson defense dealt double blow in civil trial.
newsitem.headline: Simpson defense dealt double blow in civil trial.

text.p: A key witness in O.J. Simpson's civil trial dealt a blow to the ex-football star's defence on Wednesday when he recanted previous testimony about a cut on a bloody glove found at the murder scene.

Simpson's lawyers were also defeated in their bid to deny testimony from two experts regarding 30 additional photographs of the defendant apparently wearing Bruno Magli shoes, when an appeals court ruled the witnesses could testify in the rebuttal phase of the trial.
Simpson has denied ever owning the expensive Italian designer shoes with their distinctive soles, which FBI expert William Bodziak has said left the bloody shoeprints found at the murder scene.

With the appeals court go-ahead, Bodziak was expected to testify on Thursday that the shoes worn by Simpson in the photographs were Bruno Maglis, and former FBI photo expert Gerald Richards was expected to say the pictures were genuine.

Richards testified on Wednesday he was "100 percent certain" that a single photograph taken at the same Buffalo Bills football game by a different photographer, and showing Simpson in Bruno Magli shoes was authentic. The defence had earlier brought in its own photo analyst to say he believed it was a fake.

Meanwhile, Los Angeles police criminalist Dennis Fung said he realised his mistake in testifying last week that there was a cut on the glove found at the scene. He had been called as a defence witness on that occasion.

Appearing for the plaintiffs on Wednesday, Fung said it dawned on him the defect he had seen in a photograph of the glove that he thought was a cut, was white, whereas the lining of the glove, which he thought he had seen through the cut, was brown.
Asked by plaintiffs' attorney Tom Lambert if he had lied to the jury last week about seeing the cut in the photograph, Fung replied, "I didn't lie, but I was mistaken."

At issue was the key point raised by the defence that according to Fung's previous testimony, when he entered the left-hand glove into evidence shortly after the June 12, 1994, murders of Simpson's ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman, it had a cut on it.

But the glove that was subsequently produced at the criminal trial and again in the civil trial had no cut. The defence has suggested that the glove, as well as the right glove found at Simpson's mansion, were planted by police.

"That (murder scene) glove had to have been switched because there was no damage there, was there?" defence attorney Robert Baker asked Fung on Wednesday. Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki sustained an objection to the question and the witness did not have to answer.

Fung, who has often seemed confused during his three trips to the witness stand during the civil trial and his extensive questioning during the criminal trial, refused to change his testimony on Wednesday despite pressure from Baker. "I had been in error (in identifying the cut)," he told Baker at one point.
FBI expert Richards identified the white blemish seen in the photograph on one of the glove's fingers as debris, such as soil, sitting on top of the leather.
Simpson was acquitted in October 1995 of the murders and is now battling a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the families of the victims.

The defence's evidence-planting theory appeared to be further dented when Richard Fox, a consultant forensic expert, said there were any number of ways blood could have been transferred from one side of Simpson's socks to the other.

Simpson's lawyers had contended through their own experts that with Simpson's ankles in the way, such a transfer was impossible and that the blood, identified as Nicole Brown Simpson's, must have been planted. The socks were seized by police from Simpson's bedroom the day after the murders.
